content: Dry eyes occur when there is an insufficient production of tears. Tears are essential for maintaining proper lubrication of the eyes and for removing debris or foreign particles. If you have dry eyes, you may experience a burning, scratching, or stinging sensation. Your eyes may feel fatigued or strained, particularly after reading, even for short durations. Contact lens wearers often find their lenses uncomfortable when experiencing dry eyes. Prolonged dry eye conditions can result in small abrasions on the surface of the eyes. There are several common causes of dry eyes, including: The natural aging process. Smoking or being exposed to second-hand smoke. The use of certain medications, such as cold or allergy remedies. Eye injuries or structural issues with the eyes or eyelids, such as drooping eyelids or bulging eyes. Sjögren's syndrome, a condition characterized by dryness of the eyes, mouth, and mucous membranes, often accompanied by rheumatoid arthritis or other joint disorders. A history of previous eye surgeries. It is important to seek immediate medical attention if: Your eyes become red or painful. You notice flaking, discharge, or lesions on your eyes or eyelids. You have experienced trauma to the eye, or if you have a bulging eye or a drooping eyelid. You experience joint pain, swelling, or stiffness. You also have symptoms of a dry mouth. Use artificial tears, which are available as drops or ointments. Ointments provide longer-lasting relief but may cause temporary blurry vision due to their thicker consistency. Use a humidifier, particularly during the winter months. Make a conscious effort to blink more frequently. Take regular breaks to rest your eyes. If you seek medical care for dry eyes, your healthcare provider will take a detailed medical history and perform a thorough physical examination, including an eye examination. To better understand your condition, they may ask questions such as: How long have you been experiencing dry eyes? Are both eyes affected or just one? Is the dryness constant, or does it occur only during specific activities, times, or in certain environments? Does the dryness seem to be triggered by factors like wind, dust, chemicals, sunlight, or bright light? Does it interfere with your vision or cause pain? Do your eyelids close completely and easily? Have you noticed any discharge from your eyes? Are there any factors that worsen or improve your symptoms? Have you tried artificial tears, and if so, were they effective? Are you currently taking any medications? If so, which ones? Have you had any surgeries or injuries involving your eyes or nose? Do you have any known allergies? Have you recently started using new cosmetics? Are you experiencing any other symptoms, such as a dry mouth or joint pain? Your healthcare provider may also perform specific tests to evaluate tear production and diagnose dry eyes. Artificial tears or other treatments may be prescribed based on the findings.
